problem: Pick $x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { k } \in A _ { n }$ (the alternating group on $n$ letters) at random. Is it true that, almost surely as $n \to \infty$ , the random walk on this set of generators and their inverses equidistributes in time $O ( n \log n )$ ?
comment:
The statement is one equivalent form of what it means to be an expanding set of generators. This may even be true for $k = 2$ , although it is not known if this statement is true for any pair of elements in $A _ { n }$ .

The statement about equidistribution of the random walk is one of the known equivalent definitions of being an expanding set of generators. Thus an alternative formulation of the question is: do $k$ random elements of $A _ { n }$ form an expanding set of generators?

At present this seems a pretty hopeless problem. It would imply that (a.s. as $n  \infty$ ) the diameter of $A _ { n }$ with respect to the generating set $x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { k }$ is $O ( n \log n )$ . By contrast, the best known upper bound for this is $O ( n ^ { 2 } \log ^ { C } n )$ , due to Helfgott, Seress and Zuk [171].

[171] H. A. Helfgott, A. Seress and A. Zuk, Random generators of the symmetric group: diameter, mixing time and spectral gap, J. Algebra 421 (2015), 349–368.

problem: Let $A$ be a set of size $n$ integers. Is there some $\theta$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { a \in A } \cos ( a \theta ) \leqslant - c \sqrt { n } \sin ^ { \ } } \end{array}$ ?
comment:
This is Chowla’s cosine problem. First posed explicitly in 1965 [69], it has its genesis in a question from 1948 asked by Ankeny and Chowla.

The best known result is due to Ruzsa [264], who showed that $- e ^ { - c { \sqrt { \log n } } }$ is attainable. Ruzsa remarked to me in 2001 that almost nothing is known for the more general sum of cosines $\lambda _ { 1 } \cos { r _ { 1 } t } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \lambda _ { n } \cos { r _ { n } t }$ in which $\lambda _ { 1 } , \ldots , \lambda _ { n } \in [ 0 . 9 9 , 1 . 0 1 ]$ (say).

Update 2025. There has been spectacular progress on this problem, with independent works of Bedert [29] and Jin, Milojević, Tomon, and Zhang [180] establishing bounds of the form $- \Omega ( n ^ { c } )$ for $c > 0$ ; Bedert shows that any $c < \frac { 1 } { 7 }$ is admissible.

There is a corresponding problem for sines, but it is somewhat more obscure. The question here is whether there is some $\theta$ such that $\textstyle | \sum _ { a \in A } \sin ( a \theta ) | \geqslant n ^ { 1 / 2 + c }$ . Montgomery [230, Problem 54] attributes this question to Bohr. So far as I am aware, the best example known is of a set showing that we cannot take $\begin{array} { r } { c \geqslant \frac { 1 } { 6 } } \end{array}$ , due to Bourgain in a somewhat difficult to find paper [45]. By contrast, Konyagin [199] has shown that there is some $\theta$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { | \sum _ { a \in A } \sin ( a \theta ) | \gg n ^ { 1 / 2 } ( \log n / \log \log n ) ^ { 1 / 2 } } \end{array}$ .

See also the remarks to Problem 1, where related problems are discussed with cos replaced by piecewise constant functions $f$ .

[69] S. Chowla, Some Applications of a Method of A. Selberg, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 217 (1965), 128–132.

[264] I. Z. Ruzsa, Negative values of cosine sums, Acta Arith. 111 (2004), no. 2, 179–186.

[29] B. Bedert, Polynomial bounds for the Chowla Cosine Problem, https://arxiv.org/abs/ 2509.05260.

[180] Z. Jin, A. Milojević, I. Tomon and S. Zhang, From small eigenvalues to large cuts, and Chowla’s cosine problem, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03490.

[45] J. Bourgain, Sur les sommes de sinus, Harmonic analysis: study group on translationinvariant Banach spaces, Exp. No. 3, 9 pp., Publ. Math. Orsay 83, 1, Univ. Paris XI, Orsay, 1983.

[199] S. V. Konyagin, Estimates of maxima of sine sums, East J. Approx. 3 (1997), no. 1, 63–70.

problem: Let $A \subset \mathbf { Z }$ be a set of size $n$ . For how many $\theta \in \mathbf { R } / \mathbf { Z }$ must we have $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { a \in A } \cos ( a \theta ) = 0 } \end{array}$ ?
comment:
This is [212, Problem 22]. He says ‘probably $n - 1$ , or not much less’. This is false (depending on how one defines ‘not much less’): there are examples with at most $n ^ { 5 / 6 + o ( 1 ) }$ zeros, due to Borwein, Erdélyi, Ferguson and Lockhart [43]. This

has recently been improved to $O ( n ^ { 2 / 3 } \log ^ { 2 / 3 } n )$ by Juškevičius and Sahasrabudhe [184].

It is known (see [105, 267]) that the number of zeros does tend to infinity with $n$ , albeit very slowly (the bound $( \log \log \log n ) ^ { 1 / 2 - o ( 1 ) }$ is obtained by Sahasrabudhe [267], and this has been improved to $( \log \log n ) ^ { 1 - o ( 1 ) }$ by Bedert [27]).

[43] P. Borwein, T. Erdélyi, R. Ferguson and R. Lockhart, On the zeros of cosine polynomials: solution to a problem of Littlewood, Ann. of Math. (2) 167 (2008), no. 3, 1109–1117.

[184] T. Juškevičius and J. Sahasrabudhe, Cosine polynomials with few zeros, Bull. Lond. Math. Soc. 53 (2021), no. 3, 877–892.

[267] J. Sahasrabudhe, Counting zeros of cosine polynomials: on a problem of Littlewood, Adv. Math. 343 (2019), 495–521.

[27] B. Bedert, An improved lower bound for a problem of Littlewood on the zeros of cosine polynomials, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.16075.

problem: Describe the rough structure of sets $A \subset \mathbf { Z }$ with $| A | \ = \ n$ and $\| \hat { 1 } _ { A } \| _ { 1 } \leqslant K \log n$ .
comment:
This is the ‘inverse Littlewood problem’; Littlewood conjectured, and McGehee-Pigno-Smith and Konyagin indepently proved, that $\| \hat { 1 } _ { A } \| _ { 1 } \gg \log n$ . It is natural to conjecture that $A$ has symmetric difference $o ( n )$ with a ± combination of $O _ { K } ( 1 )$ characteristic functions of progressions. More precise conclusions should presumably be possible, but one has to be careful: for instance, if $P$ is a 2-dimensional progression with sidelength $\sim e ^ { \sqrt { \log n } }$ then $\| \hat { 1 } _ { S } \| _ { 1 } \ll \log n$ .

A solution to this problem would be extremely relevant to Problem 1, as mentioned there, as well as to the further problems (1.1), (1.2) mentioned in the remarks to that problem. It may also be relevant (and it would be good to have a formal deduction of this type) to the currently unresolved Strong Littlewood Conjecture, which states that $\begin{array} { r } { \| \hat { 1 } _ { A } \| _ { 1 } \geqslant ( 1 + o ( 1 ) ) \| \hat { 1 } _ { P } \| _ { 1 } = ( \frac { 4 } { \pi ^ { 2 } } + o ( 1 ) ) \log n } \end{array}$ , where $P$ is a progression of length $n$ . (In fact, I believe that the even stronger statement $\lVert \hat { 1 } _ { A } \rVert _ { 1 } \geqslant \lVert \hat { 1 } _ { P } \rVert _ { 1 }$ is thought to hold.)

There are also interesting questions of this type in finite fields. For example, if $A \subset \mathbf { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n }$ has $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { r } | \hat { 1 } _ { A } ( r ) | \leqslant M } \end{array}$ then Sanders [272] showed $1 _ { A }$ is a $\pm$ sum of $\exp ( M ^ { 3 + o ( 1 ) } )$ indicator functions of cosets. However, the true dependence may well be polynomial.

Let us also mention the ‘Littlewood–Gowers problem’: if $A \subset \mathbf { Z } / p \mathbf { Z }$ has density $\frac { \mathrm { 1 } } { \mathrm { 2 } }$ , what is the smallest possible value of $\textstyle \sum _ { r } | { \hat { 1 } } _ { A } ( r ) |$ ? The example of an arithmetic progression shows that it can be $\ll \log p$ , but the best known lower bound is $\gg ( \log p ) ^ { 1 / 2 - \varepsilon }$ , due to Sanders [269].

[272] T. Sanders, Boolean functions with small spectral norm, revisited, Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 167 (2019), no. 2, 335–344.

[269] T. Sanders, The Littlewood-Gowers problem., J. Anal. Math. 101 (2007), 123–162.

problem: Is there a function $f : \{ 1 , \dots , N \} \to \{ - 1 , 1 \}$ with $| { \hat { f } } ( \theta ) | \geqslant$ $c \sqrt { N }$ for all $\theta$ ?
comment:
This problem is more usually stated in terms of polynomials: is there a polynomial $\begin{array} { r } { P ( z ) = \sum _ { i = 0 } ^ { N - 1 } \varepsilon _ { i } z ^ { i } } \end{array}$ with $\pm 1$ coefficients such that $| P ( z ) | \geqslant c \sqrt { N }$ for all $z$ on the unit circle? Note that a random choice of $P$ fails to work quite dramatically (there are $z$ with $| P ( z ) | \sim N ^ { - 1 / 2 + o ( 1 ) }$ , as shown by Konyagin [198]; this is basically a kind of manifestation of the ‘birthday paradox’.)

Update 2019. This problem, though not the further problems below, has now been solved in very nice work of Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe and Tiba [18].

This is a weak version of a fairly notorious problem of Littlewood, which asks whether there is in fact such a polynomial with $| P ( z ) | = ( 1 + o ( 1 ) ) \sqrt { N }$ always; the answer to this may well be no. In fact, it is conjectured (the ‘merit factor problem of Golay’) that $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } | P ( z ) | ^ { 4 } d z \geqslant ( 1 + c ) N ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ for some universal $c > 0$ . See [44] for much more information on this, which is again a somewhat notorious open problem.

Continuing the ‘ultra-flat’ theme but in a somewhat different context, I am not sure if it known whether or not there exists, for infinitely many $q$ , a subset $A \subset \mathbf { Z } / q \mathbf { Z }$ of size $\sim \boldsymbol { q } ^ { 1 / 3 }$ , all of whose nontrivial Fourier coefficients have size $O ( q ^ { 1 / 6 } )$ . (Note that $O ( q ^ { 1 / 6 } \log q )$ follows quite easily from a random construction.) This is very closely related to [230, Problem 13], where it is observed (by Ruzsa) that Sidon sets give examples of size $\sim q ^ { 1 / 2 }$ .

Finally, let me mention that, so far as I am aware, it is not known that the Liouville function $\lambda$ (restricted to $\lfloor N \rfloor$ ) does not have this property, though it surely does not since one expects it to behave somewhat like a random sequence of $\pm 1$ signs. In fact I am not sure even sure that $\lambda$ is known not to satisfy the stronger property $| \textstyle \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { N } \lambda ( n ) e ^ { 2 \pi i n \theta } | \textstyle = ( 1 + o ( 1 ) ) \sqrt { N }$ . Consideration of the fourth moment is tempting here, but it is unclear to me how to bound it from below. Zachary Chase (personal communication) remarked to me that this property must fail at either $N$ or $2 N$ , on account of the relation $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n \leqslant 2 N } \lambda ( n ) + \sum _ { n \leqslant 2 N } \lambda ( n ) e ^ { \pi \imath n } = - 2 \sum _ { n \leqslant N } \lambda ( n ) } \end{array}$ .

[198] S. V. Konyagin, On the minimum modulus of random trigonometric polynomials with coefficients ±1, Mat. Zametki 56 (1994), no. 3, 80–101, 158; translation in Math. Notes 56 (1994), no. 3–4, 931–947 (1995).

[18] P. Balister, B. Bollobás, R. Morris, J. Sahasrabudhe and M. Tiba, Flat Littlewood Polynomials exist, Ann. of Math. (2) 192 (2020), no. 3, 977–1004.

[44] P. Borwein and M. J. Mossinghoff, Barker sequences and flat polynomials, Number theory and polynomials, 71–88, London Math. Soc. Lecture Note Ser., 352, Cambridge Univ. Press, Cambridge, 2008.

problem: Suppose that $A$ is an open subset of $[ 0 , 1 ] ^ { 2 }$ with measure $\alpha$ . Are there four points in $A$ determining an axis-parallel rectangle with area $\geqslant \thinspace c \alpha ^ { 2 }$ ?
comment:
This is often known as ‘Carbery’s rectangle problem’, though it appears in a joint paper of Carbery, Christ and Wright. See [63, Section 6]. It is quite easy to show using Cauchy-Schwarz that there must be such a rectangle with area $\gg \alpha ^ { 2 } ( \log 1 / \alpha ) ^ { - 1 }$ . In the other direction, the example of a diagonal stripe of width $\sim \alpha$ shows that one could not hope for better. A related discrete problem is as follows: does there exist a set $A \subset [ N ]$ , $| A | \geqslant 1 0 0 \sqrt { N }$ , such that if an additive quadruple $x , x + h _ { 1 } , x + h _ { 2 } , x + h _ { 1 } + h _ { 2 }$ lies in $A$ then $| h _ { 1 } | | h _ { 2 } | \leqslant N$ ?

Problem 85 and related problems are considered by Keleti [193]. One might instead ask for an axis parallel rectangle $R$ , all four vertices in $A$ , and with $| A \cap R | \gg$ $\alpha ^ { C }$ . It is known that there is such an $R$ with $C = 4$ , but this need not be so with $C = 3$ , an example Keleti attributes to Reiman.

In dimension 3 and above, these problems are wide open, even without any restriction the area (volume) of cuboids. In particular one may formulate the ‘box

problem’: what is the largest density of a subset of $[ n ] ^ { 3 }$ not containing the eight vertices of a cuboid? The answer is between $n ^ { - 1 / 3 }$ and $n ^ { - 1 / 4 }$ (up to constants): see [188]. Note that this problem is essentially a hypergraph Túran problem, that of determining $\exp ( n , K _ { 2 , 2 , 2 } ^ { 3 } )$ in the language used there. As such, it goes back to questions raised by Erdős in 1965. It seems to be believed (cf. [232, Conjecture 1.4]) that the upper bound represents the truth. A recent reference, giving a new construction of the $n ^ { - 1 / 3 }$ lower bound of [188], improved lower bounds in higher dimensions and a useful overview of the literature, is [83].

[193] T. Keleti, Density and covering properties of intervals of $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ , Mathematika 47 (2000), no. 1-2, 229–242 (2002).

[188] N. H. Katz, E. Krop and M. Maggioni, Remarks on the box problem, Math. Res. Lett. 9 (2002), no. 4, 515–519.

[83] D. Conlon, C. Pohoata and D. Zahkarov, Random multilinear maps and the Erdős box problem, Discrete Analysis, 2021:17, 8pp.

problem: Let $p ( k )$ be the limit as $n  \infty$ of the probability that a random permutation on $[ n ]$ preserves some set of size $k$ . Is $p ( k )$ a decreasing function of $k$ ? Is $p ( k ) = ( C + o ( 1 ) ) k ^ { - \alpha } ( \log k ) ^ { - 3 / 2 }$ for some absolute constant $C$ ?
comment:
I first learned of this problem from a paper of Britnell and Wildon [57]. In a joint paper with Eberhard and Ford [95] it was proven that $p ( k )$ is bounded above and below by constant multiples of $k ^ { - \alpha } ( \log k ) ^ { - 3 / 2 }$ , which of course makes the second question very reasonable. This second question is a model for the following natural question: how many distinct elements are there in the $N \times N$ multiplication table?

It is quite easy to see, given known results about the Poisson behaviour of permutations, that

$$
p (k) = 1 - \sum_ {(a _ {1}, \dots , a _ {k}) \in \Omega_ {k}} \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {k} e ^ {- 1 / i} \frac {(1 / i) ^ {a _ {i}}}{a _ {i} !},
$$

where $\Omega _ { k }$ is the (finite) set of all tuples of non-negative integers for which $a _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } +$ $2 a _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + k a _ { k } ^ { \prime } \neq k$ whenever $a _ { i } ^ { \prime } \leqslant a _ { i }$ . For example, $\Omega _ { 1 } = \{ ( 0 ) \}$ , so $\textstyle p ( 1 ) = 1 - { \frac { 1 } { e } }$ .

Here is a related model problem (the relation becomes clearer upon studying [95]). Pick a random set of integers $A$ by including $i$ in $A$ with probability $\frac { 1 } { i \log { 2 } }$ . (Thus $A$ is a random lacunary sequence, with growth rate like that of the powers of 2). Let $\Sigma ( A )$ be the set of all finite sums of distinct elements of $A$ . Is it true that ${ \frac { 1 } { n } } \mathbf { E } | \Sigma ( A ) \cap [ n ] | \sim C ( \log n ) ^ { - 1 / 2 }$ as $n \to \infty$ ?

Update 2025. At a meeting in Oberwolfach in November 2025, Sawhney announced a solution (in joint work with me) to this problem and the multiplication table problem itself. We show that $p ( k ) = ( 1 + o ( 1 ) ) f ( \{ \log _ { 2 } k \} ) k ^ { - \alpha } ( \log k ) ^ { - 3 / 2 }$

where $f \in C ^ { \infty } ( \mathbf { R } / \mathbf { Z } )$ satisfies $\frac { \operatorname* { m a x } f } { \operatorname* { m i n } f } \leqslant 1 + 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 7 }$ and $f$ is ‘presumably’ not constant, though we cannot prove this latter fact.

[57] J. R. Britnell and M. Wildon, Computing derangement probabilities of the symmetric group acting on k-sets, https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.04106.

[95] S. Eberhard, K. Ford and B. Green, Permutations fixing a k-set, Int. Math. Res. Not. IMRN 2016, 21, 6713–6731.

problem: Consider a set $S \subset [ N ] ^ { 3 }$ with the property that any two distinct elements $s , s ^ { \prime }$ of $S$ are comparable, which means that $s - s ^ { \prime }$ has either two (strictly) positive indices or two (strictly) negative ones. Is $\vert S \vert \leqslant N ^ { 2 - \delta }$ for some $\delta > 0$ ?
comment:
This is perhaps the most basic of a host of questions considered by Gowers and Long [131], motivated by a question of Po-Shen Loh. It can be formulated as a question about the maximum independent set in a graph on vertex set $[ n ] ^ { 3 }$ in which two vertices $x , y$ are joined if $x , y$ are not comparable, which means that $( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , x _ { 3 } )$ is joined to (for example) all $( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } , x _ { 3 } ^ { \prime } )$ with $x _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } < x _ { 2 }$ and $x _ { 3 } ^ { \prime } > x _ { 3 }$ . One reason the problem is hard (it seems to me) is that it asks to go below the threshold for which a spectral bound (‘Delsarte’s method’) on the independence number might be possible.

Here is a modular version which, while not as natural, has a similar flavour and more symmetry. Let $S \subset \mathbf { F } _ { p } ^ { 3 }$ be set consisting of all triples $( 0 , y , z )$ where $y , - z \in \{ 1 , \ldots , \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( p - 1 ) \}$ , together with the other five similar classes (e.g. $( z , 0 , y )$ satisfying the same property). Suppose that $A - A$ is disjoint from $S$ . Is $| A | \leqslant p ^ { 2 - \delta } ?$

problem: Let $A \subset \mathbf { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n }$ . If $V$ is a subspace of ${ \bf { F } } _ { 2 } ^ { n }$ , write $\alpha ( V )$ for the density of $A$ on $V$ . Is there some $V$ of moderately small codimension on which $\alpha$ is stable in the sense that $| \alpha ( V ) - \alpha ( V ^ { \prime } ) | \leqslant \varepsilon$ whenever $V ^ { \prime }$ is a codimension 1 subspace of $V$ ?
comment:
This is an arithmetic variant of an open question in graph theory raised by Conlon and Fox [80, Lemma 3.6]. In that lemma, they show that every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices contains an $\varepsilon$ -regular subset on $n ^ { \prime }$ vertices, where $n ^ { \prime } / n \geqslant$ 2−ε−(10/ε)4 , $2 ^ { - \varepsilon ^ { - ( 1 0 / \varepsilon ) ^ { 4 } } }$ and they go on to say ‘while our bound gives a double exponential dependence, we suspect that the truth is more likely to be a single exponential. We leave this as an open problem.’

Manners showed that one can have such a $V$ of codimension exponential in $1 / \varepsilon$ . In the other direction, there are examples to show that the codimension must grow like a power of $1 / \varepsilon$ .

problem: Take a random graph $G ( n , { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } )$ . Is there almost surely a bipartition of $G$ into two sets of $n / 2$ vertices with the property that 99% of vertices have more neighbours on their own side than on the other?
comment:
Told to me by Benny Sudakov, this question was apparently asked by Füredi in 1988.

Update 2021. Ferber, Kwan, Narayanan, Sah and Sawhney [118] have shown that this is indeed true. However (personal communication) they believe it is possible that the result is true with 99 percent replaced by 100 percent. That is, is there almost surely a bipartition of $G$ into two sets of $n / 2$ vertices with the property that all vertices have more neighbours on their own side than on the other?

Update 2023. Minzer, Sah and Sawhney [229] have comprehensively dispatched this problem, in fact finding a critical value of $\gamma \approx 0 . 1 7 5 6 6$ such that almost surely there is a bipartition in which every vertex has $\geqslant ( \gamma - o ( 1 ) ) { \sqrt { n } }$ more neighbours in its own part than in the other part.

problem: I have a string $x \in \{ 0 , 1 \} ^ { n }$ . Let $\tilde { x }$ be the random string obtained by deleting bits from $x$ independently at random with probability $\frac { 1 } { 2 }$ (thus, for example, if $n = 8$ and $x = 0 0 1 1 0 1 1 0$ , it might be the case that $\tilde { x } = 0 1 1 1$ , generated by deleting bits $2 , 3 , 5 , 8$ .) An instance of $\ddot { x }$ is called a ‘trace’. How many independent traces $\ddot { x } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \ddot { x } _ { m }$ are needed before one can reconstruct $x$ with probability 0.9?
comment:
This problem is known as the trace reconstruction problem. I heard it from Yuval Peres in 2012, but it goes back to work of Levenshtein from the early 2000s. Independent work of Nazarov-Peres [234] and of De-O’Donnell-Servedio [88] on the topic gives the best known upper bound, showing that m = eCn1/3 $m = e ^ { C n ^ { 1 / 3 } }$ suffices. Update 2020. Chase [68] has improved this to en1/5 logC n. $e ^ { n ^ { 1 / 5 } \log ^ { C } n }$

Simple examples (see [23, §4.2]) show that $m$ must grow at least linearly in $n$ , and very recently Zachary Chase [67], improving on work of Holden and Lyons [174], improved this to $m \geqslant n ^ { 3 / 2 } ( \log n ) ^ { - 1 6 }$ .

A related wide-open problem is that of reconstructing a binary string of length $n$ from the multiset of all $\textstyle { \binom { n } { k } }$ substrings of length $k$ , the so-called $k$ -deck. In [204], it is shown that $k \geqslant C \sqrt { n }$ suffices (see also [277] for a different proof of a bound weaker by only a logarithm). In [91], it is shown that $k \geqslant e ^ { c { \sqrt { \log n } } }$ may not be enough (I thank Zachary Chase for these references).

problem: Is a random polynomial with coefficients in $\{ 0 , 1 \}$ and nonzero constant term almost surely irreducible?
comment:
More precisely, writing $p _ { n }$ for the probability that $1 + a _ { 1 } x + \cdot \cdot +$ $a _ { n - 1 } x ^ { n - 1 } + x ^ { n }$ is irreducible, where the $a _ { i }$ are i.i.d. Bernouilli random variables, does $p _ { n } \to 1$ ?

Unconditionally, the best bound known is $p _ { n } \gg 1 / \log n$ , due to Konyagin [200]. Very recently Breuillard and Varjú [52] have established the conjecture conditional upon the Grand Riemann Hypothesis. It should also be noted that Bary-Soroker and Kozma [22] gave an unconditional proof of the corresponding result in which the $a _ { i }$ are selected uniformly from $\{ 1 , \ldots , 2 1 0 \}$ . This depends on 210 being the product of four primes, and so their argument does not apply with 211.

Update 2023. Bary-Soroker, Koukoulopoulos and Kozma [21, Theorem 1] have made further progression on this question, establishing a corresponding result with $\{ 1 , 2 , \ldots , 2 1 0 \}$ replaced by $\{ 0 , 1 , \ldots , M \}$ for any $M \geqslant 3 4$ (and so, in particular, answering the question above with $M = 2 1 1$ ). Moreover, they prove a positive lower bound $\delta$ on the irreducibility probability of a random polynomial with coefficients in $\{ 0 , 1 , \ldots , M \}$ for all $1 \leqslant M \leqslant 3 3$ . It is also worth remarking on the short paper [20], where it is shown that a random polynomial with coefficients in $\{ \pm 1 \}$ has irreducibility probability tending to 1 along a certain infinite sequence of degrees $n$ .

problem: Are a positive proportion of positive integers a sum of two palindromes?
comment:
Of course one must specify a base $g$ (say $g = 1 0$ ) in which one is working.

Baxter, Cilleruelo and Luca [24] have shown that in base $g \geqslant 5$ , every positive integer is a sum of three palindromes. They also show that for $g \geqslant 2$ the number of $n \leqslant X$ which are the sum of two palindromes is $\geqslant X e ^ { - c _ { g } \sqrt { \log X } }$ , and for $g \geqslant 3$ is at most $( 1 - c _ { g } ) X$ , where $c _ { g } > 0$ . They also raise the question of whether this set has positive density.

They remark that it would be interesting to extend their result on sums of three palindromes to the bases $g = 2 , 3 , 4$ . They suggest that for $g = 3 , 4$ the same result should hold, but when $g = 2$ they observe that $1 0 1 1 0 0 0 0 _ { 2 }$ is not the sum of two or three palindromes. The arguably more interesting question of what can be said if one allows finitely many exceptions is not raised in the paper.

Update 2024. D. Zakharov [309] has shown that the answer to Problem 95 is negative, showing that the number of $n \leqslant X$ which are the sum of two base $g$ palindromes is $\leqslant X / \log ^ { c } X$ for some constant $c > 0$ . There remains the question of narrowing the gap between this and the result of [24] mentioned above.

[24] L. Baxter, J. Cilleruelo and F. Luca, Every positive integer is a sum of three palindromes, Math. Comp. 87 (2018), no. 314, 3023–3055.

[309] D. Zakharov, Most integers are not a sum of two palindromes, manuscript.

problem: Is every set $\Lambda \subset \mathbf { Z }$ either a Sidon set, or a set of analyticity?
comment:
This problem, known as the Dichotomy Problem, was raised in the 1960s in the subject of commutative harmonic analysis. It is important to note that the notion of Sidon set here is not the one featured in Section 4, but rather the harmonic analysis notion: $\Lambda$ is Sidon if and only if the Fourier algebra $A ( \Lambda ) =$ $\{ ( { \hat { f } } ( \lambda ) ) _ { \lambda \in \Lambda } : f \in L ^ { 1 } ( \mathbf { T } ) \}$ coincides with $c _ { 0 } ( \Lambda )$ , the algebra of sequences tending to zero. By contrast, $\Lambda$ is a set of analyticity if only analytic functions $F ^ { \prime }$ act on $A ( \Lambda )$ . Much of the classical literature on these problems is difficult to penetrate for a modern reader (at least, it is for me). For more on the problem, I recommend, at least to the reader with passable French, the relatively recent paper of Kahane and Katznelson [185]. In that paper they show that a random set $\Lambda$ in which $\mathbf { P } ( n \in \Lambda ) = p _ { n }$ is almost surely Sidon if $n p _ { n }$ is bounded, and almost surely a set of analyticity if $n p _ { n }  \infty$ .

A beautiful open question is whether every Sidon subset of $\mathbf { Z }$ (in the commutative harmonic analysis sense) is a finite union of independent sets, that is to say sets $A \subset \mathbf { Z }$ , all of whose finite subset sums are distinct (for example, the powers of two). In celebrated work from the 1980s, Pisier [246] showed that $S \subset \mathbf { Z }$ is Sidon if and only if it has the following property (⋆): there is a $\delta > 0$ such that, if $S ^ { \prime } \subset S$ is finite, then $S ^ { \prime }$ contains an independent set $A$ with $| A | \geqslant \delta | S ^ { \prime } |$ . The open question is then the completely combinatorial question of whether every set with property $( \star )$ is a finite union of independent sets. I should say that I am not sufficiently expert on these topics to say with any certainty what the relationship (if any) between this question and the dichotomy problem is.

I included this problem here in memory of Jean Bourgain, who once told me he considered it a beautiful open question, and lamented that it might never be solved since to a large extent the subject had fallen out of fashion. Let me conclude these comments with another question of Bourgain, asked to Péter Varjú in 2013 [312]: Is it possible to find $n$ points in the unit square such that the $1 / n$ -neighborhood of any line contains no more than $C$ of them for some absolute constant $C$ ? More information on this question may be found in [89].

[185] J. P. Kahane and Y. Katznelson, Entiers aléatoires et analyse harmonique, J. Anal. Math. 105 (2008), 363–378.

[246] G. Pisier, Arithmetic characterizations of Sidon sets, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (N.S.) 8 (1983), no. 1, 87–89.

[312] (Various authors) Remembering Jean Bourgain (1954–2018), Notices Amer. Math. Soc. 68 (2021), no. 6, 942–957.

[89] C. Demeter and R. Zhang, On the $N$ -set occupancy problem, Results Math. 80 (2025), no. 8, Paper No. 239.

problem: In how many ways (asymptotically) $Q ( n )$ may $n$ non-attacking queens be placed on an $n \times n$ chessboard?
comment:
This is the $n$ queens problem. Though very recreational in its statement, it certainly hides some interesting mathematics. This is most clearly seen for the ‘modular’ version of the problem, in which the chessboard is toroidal and one defines $T ( n )$ to be the number of ways to place $n$ non-attacking queens on an $n \times n$ board.

There has been significant recent progress on the problem of estimating $Q ( n )$ and $T ( n )$ . Regarding the former, Simkin [284] showed that $Q ( n ) = ( ( 1 + o ( 1 ) ) n e ^ { - \alpha } ) ^ { n }$ , where $\alpha \approx 1 . 9 4 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 }$ is a constant given in terms of an entropy optimisation problem. Simkin’s bounds on $\alpha$ have been tightened to $\alpha \in \lfloor 1 . 9 4 4 0 0 0 7 5 2 , 1 . 9 4 4 0 0 1 0 8 2 \rfloor$ by Agrawal, Boyd and Nobel [5] but an explicit solution remains an open problem). Using very different methods, in a monumental paper Bowtell and Keevash [49] showed that $T ( n ) = ( ( 1 + o ( 1 ) ) n e ^ { - 3 } ) ^ { n }$ when $n \equiv 1$ or 5 modulo 6 (there are no configurations in the other cases).

The problem of obtaining an asymptotic (rather than an asymptotic for the log) remains open. In the toroidal case, the problem is equivalent to the following. Identify $( \mathbf { Z } / n \mathbf { Z } ) ^ { n }$ with the space of functions $f : \{ 1 , . . . , n \} \ \to \ \mathbf { Z } / n \mathbf { Z }$ , and let $S \subset ( \mathbf { Z } / n \mathbf { Z } ) ^ { n }$ be the set of bijections. How many pairs $( \pi _ { 1 } , \pi _ { 2 } ) \in ( \mathbf { Z } / n \mathbf { Z } ) ^ { n }$ are there with $\pi _ { 1 } , \pi _ { 2 } , \pi _ { 1 } + \pi _ { 2 } , \pi _ { 1 } - \pi _ { 2 } \in S$ ?

This is, of course, very reminiscent of questions about four-term arithmetic progressions, and one suspects that the Gowers $U ^ { 3 }$ -norm of $1 _ { S }$ or related objects will come into play. For further comments, and for an ingenious solution to the problem in which only $\pi _ { 1 } , \pi _ { 2 }$ and $\pi _ { 1 } - \pi _ { 2 }$ are required to lie in $S$ , see [98].

[49] C. Bowtell and P. Keevash, The n-queens problem, https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.08083.

[98] S. Eberhard, F. Manners and R. Mrazovic, Additive triples of bijections, or the toroidal semiqueens problem, J. Eur. Math. Soc. (JEMS) 21 (2019), no. 2, 441–463.

problem: Let $d \geqslant 3$ be an odd integer. Give bounds on $\nu ( d )$ such that if $n > \nu ( d )$ the following is true: given any homogeneous polynomial $F ( \mathbf { x } ) \mathbf { \Psi } =$ $F ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) \in \mathbf { Z } [ x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ]$ of degree $d$ , there is some $\mathbf { x } \in \mathbf { Z } ^ { n } \setminus \{ \mathbf { 0 } \}$ such that $F ( \mathbf { x } ) = 0$ .

That $\nu ( d )$ exists at all is highly nontrivial and is a famous result of Birch [36]. It was 40 years before Wooley [307] gave the first explicit values of $\nu ( d )$ , which have tower-type growth in $d$ . So far as I am aware it is considered possible that $\nu ( d ) = d ^ { 2 }$ , but even the local variant of this (that is, finding solutions in $\mathbf { Q } _ { p }$ rather than $\mathbf { Q }$ ) is wide open (see, for instance, [169]).

It is known that $\nu ( 3 ) \leqslant 1 3$ by work of Heath-Brown [168].

Update 2025: Lampert, Snowden and Ziegler [206] have made significant progress on the variant problem with $s$ forms $F _ { 1 } , \ldots , F _ { s }$ of fixed degree $d$ , showing that the dependence is polynomial in $s$ in this setting.

problem:
As Problem 98 illustrates, finding a single solution to a polynomial equation $F ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) = C$ (say) can be very difficult, and asymptotically enumerating such solutions inside (say) a box $[ X ] ^ { n }$ is still harder. Nonetheless, one may ask about going yet further, and pose the question of estimating the number of solutions with the $x _ { i }$ constrained to lie in some set $A \subset [ X ]$ . In particular, what conditions on $A$ ensure that the number of such solutions is roughly $\alpha ^ { n }$ times the number of solutions in $[ X ]$ , where $\alpha : = | A | / X$ is the density of $A$ in $[ X ]$ , imagining here that $\alpha \in ( 0 , 1 )$ is fixed and $X$ is large?

When $F$ is linear (and $n \geqslant 3$ ) such a condition is that $A$ has no large Fourier coefficients, that is to say $\begin{array} { r } { X ^ { - 1 } \big | \sum _ { x \leqslant X } ( 1 _ { A } ( x ) - \alpha ) e ( \theta x ) \big | = o ( 1 ) } \end{array}$ uniformly in $\theta$ . Some questions are

(i) What can be said when $\deg F = 2$ and $n = 7$ , at least in the ‘generic’ case?   
(ii) What is the least value of $n$ for which one can say something in the case $\deg F = 3$ , at least in the ‘generic’ case?   
(iii) What about specific interesting cases such as $F ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , x _ { 3 } , x _ { 4 } ) = x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } +$ $x _ { 3 } ^ { 2 } + x _ { 4 } ^ { 2 }$ ?
comment:
Generic here might mean one of two different things. What happens for a ‘random’ $F$ with coefficients selected from a large box? What happens for $F ^ { \prime }$ whose coefficients lie outside some positive codimension algebraic set? I mostly have in mind the latter interpretation, which offers the chance of saying something for particular explicit $F$ , but the former case may also be interesting. In both cases one wants a conclusion for all $A$ , that is to say the allowed $F ^ { \prime }$ cannot depend on $A$ .

Regarding item (i), in the case $n = 8$ it should probably follow using the methods of [151] that in the generic case it is enough for $A$ not to correlate with progressions, i.e. $\begin{array} { r } { X ^ { - 1 } \big \vert \sum _ { x \in { \cal { X } } } ( 1 _ { \cal { A } } ( x ) - \alpha ) 1 _ { \cal { P } } ( x ) \big \vert = o ( 1 ) } \end{array}$ for all progressions $P \subset [ X ]$ , but it seems hard to reduce the number of variables to 7. On the other hand, I would guess that in the generic case $n = 5$ (or perhaps even fewer) variables should suffice for such a statement.

I know very little about (ii). Presumably, some value of $n$ could be provided by adapting the methods of Cook and Magyar [84] but this is not in the literature so far as I am aware.

Finally, (iii) seems very difficult (and it would be very interesting, as it could well shed light on the well-known problem of showing that numbers $\equiv 4 ( { \bmod { 2 4 } } )$ are $p _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + p _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + p _ { 3 } ^ { 2 } + p _ { 4 } ^ { 2 } )$ . One would certainly need to assume that $A$ has no large quadratic Fourier coefficients, $\begin{array} { r } { X ^ { - 1 } \big | \sum _ { x \leqslant X } ( 1 _ { A } ( x ) - \alpha ) e ( \theta x ^ { 2 } ) \big | = o ( 1 ) } \end{array}$ , and for the analogous question with 5 or more variables a condition of this nature is sufficient (this may be extracted from [59]).

When I prepared the first version of these notes, the following problem seemed not especially well-known. Now it seems to be considered a major unsolved problem in group theory.

problem: Is every group well-approximated by finite groups?
comment:
There are really two questions here, namely is every group sofic? and is every group hyperlinear? Here is a precise statement of the latter question. Suppose that $G$ is a group. Is the following true? For every finite set $A \subset G$ containing the identity $e _ { G }$ and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ , there is some unitary group $\mathrm { U } ( n )$

and a map $\phi : A \to \operatorname { U } ( n )$ such that $\phi ( e _ { G } ) = I _ { n }$ , such that $\phi$ is an ‘approximate homomorphism’ in the sense that $\| \phi ( a _ { 1 } a _ { 2 } ) - \phi ( a _ { 1 } ) \phi ( a _ { 2 } ) \| < \varepsilon$ for all $a _ { 1 } , a _ { 2 } \in A$ such that $a _ { 1 } a _ { 2 } \in A$ , whilst $\phi$ is ‘nontrivial’ in the sense that $\| \phi ( a ) - I _ { n } \| \geqslant 1$ for all $a \in A$ , $a \neq e _ { G }$ . (Here $\| - \|$ is the $\ell ^ { 2 }$ -to- $\ell ^ { 2 }$ operator norm. Also, the constant 1 is unimportant, since a certain amplification trick shows that the concept is the same if 1 is replaced by any other constant in $( 0 , { \sqrt { 2 } } )$ ; see [242, p. 458].)

Roughly speaking, the notion of sofic replaces the unitary group U(n) here with the symmetric group Sym $( n )$ , endowed with normalised Hamming distance. It is known that all sofic groups are hyperlinear, but the reverse implication is not known. See [242].

The Higman group $\langle a _ { 1 } , a _ { 2 } , a _ { 3 } , a _ { 4 } | a _ { i } ^ { a _ { i + 1 } } = a _ { i } ^ { 2 } , i \in \mathbf { Z } / 4 \mathbf { Z } \rangle$ (where here $x ^ { y } : = y ^ { - 1 } x y$ ) is not known to be either hyperlinear or sofic. Helfgott and Juschenko [170] showed that if the Higman group is sofic then some very strange functions $f : \mathbf { Z } / p \mathbf { Z } \to \mathbf { Z } / p \mathbf { Z }$ must exist. Namely, given $\varepsilon > 0$ , if $p$ is sufficiently large in terms of $\varepsilon$ then there is $f$ with $f ( x + 1 ) = 2 f ( x )$ for at least $( 1 - \varepsilon ) p$ values of $x \in \mathbf { Z } / p \mathbf { Z }$ , and also $f \circ f \circ f \circ f ( x ) = x$ for all $x$ .

[242] V. G. Pestov, Hyperlinear and sofic groups: a brief guide, Bull. Symbolic Logic 14 (2008), no. 4, 449–480.

[170] H. A. Helfgott and K. Juschenko, Soficity, short cycles, and the Higman group, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 371 (2019), no.4, 2771–2795.
